Recap: Continuous Batching


Dynamically batch requests at the token level, allowing for early return and better GPU utilization.
As soon as one request in the batch finishes generating its next token, it can be returned to the client, while the remaining requests continue processing.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Recap: Paged Attention


Logical blocks: The model’s attention mechanism operates on the entire context as a single logical block (e.g., a 16K token context treated as one block for attention computations).
Physical blocks (pages): Memory is divided into smaller physical blocks/pages (e.g., 16–32 tokens each), dynamically allocated and mapped to different requests as needed.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Paged KV Cache

Paged Attention 
Each request’s KV cache is divided into multiple physical blocks (pages) that can be allocated independently.
Multiple requests can share the same physical blocks if they have similar context lengths, improving memory efficiency and GPU utilization.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Paged Attention


PagedAttention allows storing continuous keys and values in non-contiguous memory space
During the attention computation, the PagedAttention kernel identifies and fetches different KV blocks separately
Computes attention across these non-contiguous blocks
This is done in a custom CUDA kernel optimized for the block-table lookup pattern

vLLM Prefix Caching
vLLM implements hash-based automatic prefix caching (enabled with --enable-prefix-caching by default):


Each KV block is hashed based on its token content
If a hash matches an existing block in the cache -> reuse it (skip prefill for those tokens)

Paper: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs - Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2024

(root)
 ├── "cat"

 └── "dog"



All seen token sequences are stored in a radix tree
Each node in the tree points to cached KV blocks in GPU memory

The Hardware Mismatch Problem
Modern GPUs are designed for training (compute-bound), but inference has asymmetric needs:


Prefill Requirements:

High FLOPS (tensor cores)
Moderate memory bandwidth

Decode Requirements:

High memory bandwidth (HBM)
Large memory capacity (for KV cache)
Lower compute acceptable






The Problem: Single GPU must satisfy both, leading to over-provisioning.

Mixing phases causes interference
Batching prefills helps utilization but increases TTFT
Batching decodes helps throughput but increases TPOT


SLO Conflicts:

TTFT (Time To First Token) requires fast prefill
TPOT (Time Per Output Token) requires uninterrupted decode
Optimizing one hurts the other

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Choosing Your Stack: Scenario-Based

Scenario 1:
“Run a chatbot on my desktop / laptop” -> llama.cpp with Q4_K_M quantization, Metal backend. Full privacy, no cloud needed.


Scenario 2:
“Serve Llama-70B to 100 concurrent users on 4× A100” -> vLLM or SGLang with tensor parallelism. Enable prefix caching for chat workloads.


Scenario 3:
“Structured JSON extraction from documents at scale” -> SGLang — RadixAttention maximizes prefix reuse for repeated templates, compressed FSM for structured output.


Scenario 4:
“Deploy DeepSeek-R1 across a 64-GPU cluster” -> NVIDIA Dynamo with disaggregated serving, vLLM or TRT-LLM backend. Smart router for KV cache locality.

title: Inference Servers - II
text:
Key Takeaways

Prefill is compute-bound, decode is memory-bound
Continuous batching (Orca) eliminates idle GPU time by scheduling at iteration level -> 2-36× throughput over static batching
PagedAttention (vLLM) eliminates KV cache fragmentation with OS-inspired virtual memory -> reduces waste from 60-80% to <4%, enabling 2-4× more throughput
Prefix caching avoids redundant prefill computation -> 5-20× TTFT reduction for workloads with shared prefixes
Disaggregated serving (DistServe) separates prefill and decode onto different GPUs -> independent optimization and 1.4-2.35× throughput improvement
Production orchestration (NVIDIA Dynamo) adds smart routing, dynamic scaling, KV cache management, and SLO-aware planning across GPU clusters -> up to 7× throughput on Blackwell

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention

Inference vs Training
Training

Weight updates via backprop & gradient descent
Parallelizable across sequence length
Optimized for throughput
Memory: weights + gradients + optimizer states + activations
\(\approx\) 4-6x model size (FP16)

Inference

Samples tokens from learned distributions - no weight updates
Optimized for latency (TTFT, ITL) and throughput simultaneously
Memory: weights + KV cache + forward pass activations
\(\approx\) 1-1.5x model size at short context; can grow much larger when KV cache dominates

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Memory : KV Cache


Multi-Head Attention Overview

\(\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\)
\[\text{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)W^O\]
Scaled Dot-Product Attention:

\(Q, K, V\): Query, Key, and Value matrices derived from input embeddings
\(d_k\): The dimensionality of the keys (and queries)
\(W^O\): Output projection matrix that combines the outputs of all heads into a single vector.
\(h\): The number of parallel attention heads.

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
MHA - Generation Phase
Generation Phase (Autoregressive Decoding):

Generate tokens one at a time autoregressively
At each step, compute attention over all previously generated tokens
Keys and Values for past tokens remain unchanged
Only the new token’s Query needs to attend to all previous Keys/Values

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
MHA - Generation Phase


Problem: Without caching, we recompute K and V for all previous tokens at every step!

Step 1: Compute K, V for token 1
Step 2: Recompute K, V for tokens 1, 2
Step 3: Recompute K, V for tokens 1, 2, 3
…
Step N: Recompute K, V for all N tokens → O(N²) redundant computation


Solution: KV Cache — Store computed K and V vectors and reuse them

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:

Reduced per-token compute from O(N) to O(1) by caching K and V for all past tokens
Reduced TTFT, increased throughput

The Key Question

Is GPU spending its time doing compute or waiting for data?


To answer this, we need to understand:

Arithmetic Intensity - how much compute per byte of memory accessed
The Roofline Model - what limits the GPU’s performance
How prefill and decode differ - why decode is memory bound

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Arithmetic Intensity
\[\text{Arithmetic Intensity} = \frac{\text{Compute FLOPs}}{\text{Memory Bytes}}\]
AI tells you whether the model is spending time computing (doing math) or fetching (moving data).

Low AI = GPU mostly waiting for data.
High AI = GPU mostly doing useful computation.







Tip


Intuition : “Imagine you’re a cook. The fridge (HBM) is in the next room. Arithmetic intensity is how many dishes you can prepare per trip to the fridge.

If AI=1, you grab one ingredient, cook one dish, walk back. Terrible.
If AI=100, you grab one ingredient and cook 100 dishes. Great!”

title: Inference Math and Efficient Attention
text:
Arithmetic Intensity
Setup: Matrix multiply in a linear layer : \(Y = X \cdot W\)
B : batch size, D : hidden dimension, F : feedforward dimension


\(X\): B \(\times\) D, \(W\): D \(\times\) F
FLOPs = \(2 \cdot B \cdot D \cdot F\)
Bytes transferred:

Read X: \(B \cdot D \cdot 2\)
Read W: \(D \cdot F \cdot 2\)
Write Y: \(B \cdot F \cdot 2\)

Total Bytes = \(2(BD + DF + BF)\)

\[\text{AI} = \frac{2 \cdot B \cdot D \cdot F}{2(BD + DF + BF)}\]
\[= \frac{B \cdot D \cdot F}{BD + DF + BF}\]
If \(B \ll D, F\):
\[\text{AI} \approx \frac{B \cdot D \cdot F}{D \cdot F} = B\]


Arithmetic intensity \(\approx\) batch size (when B is small relative to model dimensions)

Batch Size = 1 (single-stream decode)
\[    \text{AI} = \frac{2 \cdot D \cdot F}{2 \cdot D \cdot F + 2 \cdot D + 2 \cdot F} \approx 1 \text{ FLOP/byte}\]



You read the entire weight matrix (\(D \times F\))…

…but only do one row’s worth of compute



For A100 GPU (Capacity : 150-200 FLOPs/byte):

AI \(\approx\) 1 \(\ll\) 150-200
Peak-compute upper bound: < 1% of peak FLOPs
The GPU is basically spending all its time waiting for data to arrive from memory, not doing math.

The Roofline Model


Performance is bounded by:

Compute : how fast GPU does math (FLOPs/s)
Bandwidth : how fast data moves (GB/s)
Capacity : whether weights + KV cache fit at all (GB)








Note


Knee point = bandwidth-bound to compute-bound transisiton -> minimum AI needed to fully utilize GPU’s compute.







Figure: an example roofline plot showing two algorithms with different arithmetic intensities (Algo 1 and Algo 2) and their corresponding theoretical peak throughput under different bandwidths (BW1 and BW2). In the red area, an algorithm is bandwidth bound at both bandwidths and is wasting some fraction of the hardware’s peak FLOPs/s. The yellow area is bandwidth-bound only at the lower bandwidth (BW1). The green area is compute-bound at all bandwidths.


\[\text{Performance} = \min(\text{Peak FLOPs}, \text{AI} \times \text{BW})\]

Predict next token given previous tokens, i.e., learn \(P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)\)

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Auto Regressive Language Model
\[
P(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(y_t \mid y_{<t})
\]
The core objective : Predict the conditional probability distribution
\[
P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, \theta)
\]
Where:

\(y_t\): The token to be predicted at time step \(t\).
\(y_{<t} = (y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})\): The sequence of preceding tokens (context).
\(\theta\): The model parameters.

Example : P(“The cat sat”) = P(“The”) × P(“cat”|“The”) × P(“sat”|“The cat”)

Training vs. Inference

Training : Learn to predict the next token given the previous tokens
Inference : Use the trained model to generate text, given a prompt

Decoding

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Decoding

\(P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)\) gives probability distribution over next-tokens
We choose a next token, add it to the context, and get a new distribution over next-tokens
Choose next token based on some decoding strategy, and repeat until we generate an end-of-sequence token or reach a maximum length.



Token-level decoding algorithms are primarily concerned with how to choose the next token.

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Decoding

Decoding is search : Optimize for the most likely sequence of tokens given the model’s probability distribution
Different decoding strategies balance between determinism, diversity, and computational efficiency

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Greedy Decoding

Choose the most likely token at each step
May not produce the most likely overall sequence, as it doesn’t consider future tokens
Can lead to repetitive or generic outputs


Where is greedy decoding reasonable?

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Beam Search

Keep track of the top-k most likely sequences at each step, rather than just the single most likely token.
Top-k sequences are called “beams” and k is the “beam width”.

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Beam Search

At each step, expand each of the k sequences by one token and keeps the top-k resulting sequences based on their cumulative probabilities.

for seq, score in beams:
    # If the last token is EOS, keep the beam as is
    if seq[0, -1].item() == tokenizer.eos_token_id:
        all_candidates.append((seq, score))
        continue

    outputs = model(seq)
    logits = outputs.logits[0, -1, :]
    log_probs = F.log_softmax(logits, dim=-1)

    # Get top K candidates for this specific beam
    top_k_log_probs, top_k_idx = torch.topk(log_probs, beam_width)

    for i in range(beam_width):
        next_token = top_k_idx[i].unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0)
        new_seq = torch.cat([seq, next_token], dim=1)
        new_score = score + top_k_log_probs[i].item()
        all_candidates.append((new_seq, new_score))

# Sort all candidates by score and pick the top 'beam_width'
beams = sorted(all_candidates, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)[:beam_width]

Computationally expensive, but can produce higher-quality outputs

Example for GPT-2 small: B = 50,257 (vocab size) ^ 128 (max length) = 50,000^128 sequences


In practice, often used with a small beam width (e.g., B=5, 10, 20, 30) to balance quality and efficiency.

Memory intensive
Can still produce generic or repetitive outputs

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Top-k Sampling

\[\hat{y}_t \sim \begin{cases} p_\theta(y_t | y_{<t}, x) / Z_t & \text{if } y_t \in \text{top } k \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
where \(Z_t = \sum_{y \in \text{top } k} p_\theta(y | y_{<t}, x)\) is the normalization constant.

\(Z_t\) is the sum of the probabilities of the top-k tokens. It is used to renormalize the truncated distribution so that the remaining probabilities sum to 1.

Sort descending
Take cumulative sum
Find smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p
Renormalize and sample

Min-p Sampling

Top-p Downside: The threshold p is absolute - doesn’t scale with model confidence.
Min-p fix: Set a dynamic floor based on the probability of the most likely token:

\[\hat{y}_t \sim p_\theta(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x) \quad \text{if} \quad p_\theta(y_t) \geq \alpha \cdot \max_v p_\theta(v)\]
where \(\alpha\) is the min_p parameter (e.g., 0.05–0.1).
Key insight: The threshold scales with model confidence.

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Temperature Sampling

Temperature sampling: Adjust the model’s output logits by a temperature parameter T before sampling.
Instead of truncating the distribution, we can soften or sharpen it.

\[softmax(z_i , T) = \frac{e^{z_i / T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j / T}}\]
Where T is the temperature parameter applied to logits \(z_i\) (before softmax)
model.generate(do_sample=True, temperature=0.7)

Temperature is applied to logits before softmax, so it directly affects the shape of the probability distribution. In practice: T=0.7–1.0 for creative tasks, T=0.0–0.3 for code/factual tasks. Often combined with top-p.

title: Decoding & Sampling Methods
text:
Temperature Sampling


T = 1.0 : Original distribution (ancestral sampling)
T < 1.0 : More peaked, concentrated around the mode
T > 1.0 : More uniform, more diverse/random outputs
T => 0 : Equivalent to greedy decoding

text:
Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm
Almost all models post-2020 use pre-norm.

Original Transformer : Post Norm
x -> Attention(x) -> Add -> LayerNorm -> FFN -> Add -> LayerNorm
GPT 2 : Pre-Norm
x -> [LN -> Attn] -> +x -> [LN -> FFN] -> +x

title: Modern Architectures - I
text:
Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm

Why pre-norm wins:

Better gradient flow through residual connections.
Practical evidence: almost all modern LLMs use pre-norm


Note : Double norm also used in some models, but not as common as pre-norm. It applies LayerNorm both before and after the sub-layer.
Question : BERT was trained with post-norm and it was huge success. But most models use pre-norm. Why?
Ref : Xiong et al. 2020, On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture

title: Modern Architectures - I
text:
LayerNorm vs RMSNorm

Strong consensus toward RMSNorm



LayerNorm (original):
Normalize by subtracting mean and dividing by std dev, then scale (\(\gamma\)) and shift (\(\beta\)):
\[y = \frac{x - E[x]}{\sqrt{Var[x] + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma + \beta\]
Models : GPT-1/2/3, OPT, GPT-J, BLOOM

RMSNorm (modern):
Drop the mean subtraction and bias term:
\[y = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}||x||_2^2 + \epsilon}} \cdot \gamma\]
Models : LLaMA family, DeepSeek V3, Qwen3 etc

Why RMSNorm

Fewer operations: RMSNorm requires fewer computations (no mean subtraction, no bias term) which reduces both FLOPs and memory bandwidth.

title: Modern Architectures - I
section: Dropping Bias Terms in FFN and LayerNorm
text:
Dropping Bias Terms in FFN and LayerNorm
Most modern transformers have no bias terms in linear layers or LayerNorm.
Original: \(FFN(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2\)
Modern: \(FFN(x) = \sigma(xW_1)W_2\)
SiLU activation is used instead of ReLU, but the key point is that bias terms are removed.
Reasons:

Same memory/data movement argument as RMSNorm – fewer parameters to load
Optimization stability – empirically, dropping bias terms stabilizes training of very large networks

Most models use RMSNorm
Almost all models use pre-norm

Position Encodings
Why do we need Position Encodings?


Attention is a position-agnostic operation

Treats the input as a set, not a sequence
No inherent notion of order or position

Example:
The dog chased another dog vs Another dog chased the dog

Both have the same set of tokens
But different meanings

Solution: Add positional encodings to inject order information into the model

Position encoding magnitude greater than token embedding magnitude
Model should separately learn to handle content and position, which can make learning harder.

Sinusoidal Position Encoding
\[ PE_{(pos,2i)} = sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \]
\[ PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \]

title: Modern Architectures - I
text:
Sinusoidal Position Encoding
Why sin and cos?
\(sin(a+b) = sin(a)cos(b) + cos(a)sin(b)\)
\(cos(a+b) = cos(a)cos(b) - sin(a)sin(b)\)
PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos)
So
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sin(\omega \cdot (p+k)) &= \sin(\omega p)\cos(\omega k) + \cos(\omega p)\sin(\omega k)
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\cos(\omega \cdot (p+k)) &= \cos(\omega p)\cos(\omega k) - \sin(\omega p)\sin(\omega k)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Modern Architectures - I
text:
Sinusoidal Position Encoding
Downsides :
Sinusoidal PE is added to embeddings: \(x_p = x_{token} + PE(p)\)
Then projected: \(q_p = W_q x_p\), \(k_p = W_kx_p\)

Position and content are entangled before attention
Relative position is implicit, not structural
Attention must learn how to extract distance

title: Modern Architectures - I
text:
Absolute vs Relative Position Encodings

Absolute position encodings - Unique encoding to each position in the sequence.
Relative position encodings - Encodes the relative distance between tokens, rather than their absolute position.

title: Modern Architectures - I

Why do we need them?

“The cat sat” should have similar relationships whether at positions [5,6,7] or [105,106,107]
Absolute encodings make it harder to learn patterns based on relative distance (e.g., “the word two positions to the left of X”)

Benefits:

Learn patterns based on relative distance between tokens
More important for many tasks than absolute position
No reliance on fixed absolute positions

The training objective: Maximize the probability of the correct next token
Given:

Cross-entropy loss measures how well the model’s predicted probabilities match the true next tokens.

title: GPT-2 : Training
section: Cross Entropy Loss for Language Modeling
text:
Cross Entropy Loss for Language Modeling
Cross-entropy loss measures how well the model’s predicted probabilities match the true next tokens.
Mathematical Formula:
\[
\text{Loss} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P(x_i^{\text{target}})
\]
Where:

\(N\) = total number of tokens
\(P(x_i^{\text{target}})\) = predicted probability for the correct token at position \(i\)
The negative sign converts it to a loss (we want to maximize probability = minimize negative log probability)

title: GPT-2 : Training
text: Calculating Cross Entropy Loss

title: GPT-2 : Training
text:
Understanding Cross Entropy Loss
Step-by-step computation

Get logits from model: shape (batch, seq_len, vocab_size)
Apply softmax to get probabilities
Extract target probabilities: probability assigned to correct tokens
Apply logarithm: log probabilities are more numerically stable
Average over all tokens
Negate: we minimize negative log-likelihood


In PyTorch, we can compute this in one step using cross_entropy function:
# PyTorch does all 6 steps in one function:
loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits_flat, targets_flat)
Initial loss (untrained model): ~10.82
Target loss (well-trained): decreases toward a floor set by the data’s entropy (~3 for GPT-2 small)

text:
Why isn’t simple attention enough?
Simple dot-product attention has no parameters to train:

The score is just raw similarity \(x_i \cdot x_j\) - symmetric, so token i matches j exactly as much as j matches i.
Each token uses its one embedding for every role - asking, being matched, and being copied - all at once.


Fix: project each token into three specialized, learned spaces.
=> Query, Key, Value

title: Transformers - II

The fix, in code
Simple attention reuses inputs for all three roles:
attn_scores    = inputs @ inputs.T        # ask · match
attn_weights   = torch.softmax(attn_scores, dim=-1)
output_vectors = attn_weights @ inputs    # copy content

Give each role its own learned projection:
Q, K, V = inputs @ W_q, inputs @ W_k, inputs @ W_v

attn_scores    = Q @ K.T
attn_weights   = torch.softmax(attn_scores, dim=-1)
output_vectors = attn_weights @ V
Only change: raw inputs -> learned Q, K, V.

\[

\]

class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, qkv_bias=False):

        super().__init__()
        self.W_query = nn.Linear(d_in, d_out, bias=qkv_bias)
        self.W_key = nn.Linear(d_in, d_out, bias=qkv_bias)
        self.W_value = nn.Linear(d_in, d_out, bias=qkv_bias)

    def forward(self, x):
        keys = self.W_key(x)
        queries = self.W_query(x)
        values = self.W_value(x)
        attn_scores = queries @ keys.T
        attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores / keys.shape[-1]**0.5, dim=-1)
        context_vec = attn_weights @ values
        return context_vec

Multi-Head Attention : Efficient Implementation
class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, d_in, d_out, context_length, dropout, num_heads, qkv_bias=False):
    super().__init__()
    self.num_heads = num_heads
    assert d_out % num_heads == 0, "d_out must be divisible by num_heads"
    self.head_dim = d_out // num_heads
    self.out_proj = nn.Linear(d_out, d_out)

  def forward(self, X):

    queries = queries.reshape(batches, num_tokens, self.num_heads, self.head_dim) # B x L x num_heads x head_dim
    keys = keys.reshape(batches, num_tokens, self.num_heads, self.head_dim) # B x L x num_heads x head_dim
    values = values.reshape(batches, num_tokens, self.num_heads, self.head_dim) # B x L x num_heads x head_dim

    queries = queries.transpose(1, 2) # B x num_heads x L x head_dim
    keys = keys.transpose(1, 2) # B x num_heads x L x head_dim
    values = values.transpose(1, 2) # B x num_heads x L x head_dim

    attn_scores = queries @ keys.transpose(2, 3) # (B x num_heads x L x head_dim) @ (B x num_heads x head_dim x L) => B x num_heads x L x L

    # mask : # L x L => (1 x 1 x L x L)
    attn_scores.masked_fill_(self.mask.bool()[:num_tokens, :num_tokens], -torch.inf) # B x num_heads x L x L

    attn_weights = torch.softmax(attn_scores / self.head_dim ** 0.5, dim=-1) 
    attn_weights = nn.Dropout(self.dropout)(attn_weights) # B x num_heads x L x L

    context_vec = attn_weights @ values # (B x num_heads x L x L) @ (B x num_heads x L x head_dim)

    context_vec = context_vec.transpose(1, 2) # B x L x num_heads x head_dim
    context_vec = context_vec.reshape(batches, num_tokens, self.d_out) # B x L x d_out

    return self.out_proj(context_vec) # (B x L x d_out) @ (d_out x d_out) => B x L x d_out

Normalization

\[\hat x = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma + \epsilon} \]

x: input vector for a token
μ: mean of the elements in x
σ: standard deviation of the elements in x
ε: small constant for numerical stability
γ, β: learnable parameters for scaling and shifting

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Position Encodings
Why do we need Position Encodings?


Attention is a position-agnostic operation

Treats the input as a set, not a sequence
No inherent notion of order or position

Example:
The dog chased another dog vs Another dog chased the dog

Both have the same set of tokens
But different meanings

Solution: Add positional encodings to inject order information into the model

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Integer Position Encoding

Add the integer position directly into embeddings.
Problems:

Position encoding magnitude greater than token embedding magnitude
Model should separately learn to handle content and position, which can make learning harder.

title: Modern Architectures - II
text: Binary Position Encoding

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Binary Position Encoding


Problems:

Hamming distance artifacts - small position changes can flip many bits
Sparse representations (many bits are zero, which can make learning harder)
No learnable interpolation

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Sinusoidal Position Encoding
A smooth, continuous version of binary encoding.
\[ PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\big(pos/10000^{\,2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big), \qquad PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\big(pos/10000^{\,2i/d_{\text{model}}}\big) \]

Each dimension is a sine/cosine of a different frequency (like the hands of a clock)

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Why a range of frequencies?

High frequency - short wavelength: changes a lot between adjacent positions, repeats almost immediately => tiny unique range. 
Low frequency - long wavelength: adjacent positions nearly identical, repeats after long range => no resolution. 


Fix : Use many frequencies, like the bits of a number:

Fast “hands” resolve adjacent positions; slow “hands” span the whole sequence.
The base \(10000\) sets the slowest wavelength -> the longest distance you can represent.
The combined pattern repeats only after the LCM of all wavelengths -> effectively never.

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Why both sin and cos?

Relative position becomes a simple rotation.


Let \(\omega = 1/10000^{2i/d}\) \[\sin(\omega(p+k)) = \sin(\omega p)\cos(\omega k) + \cos(\omega p)\sin(\omega k)\]
\[\cos(\omega(p+k)) = \cos(\omega p)\cos(\omega k) - \sin(\omega p)\sin(\omega k)\]


These two pairs - make a point on the unit circle at angle \(\omega p\):


\[PE_\omega(p) = \big(\sin(\omega p),\ \cos(\omega p)\big)\]

title: Modern Architectures - II
Modern Architectures - II
text:
Sinusoidal PE: Downsides
PE is added to the token embedding, then projected into queries and keys:
\[x_p = x_{token} + PE(p), \qquad q_p = W_q\,x_p, \quad k_p = W_k\,x_p\]
The attention score then splits into four terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_p \cdot k_n = \;& \underbrace{(W_q x_{tok})\cdot(W_k x_{tok})}_{\text{content×content}} + \underbrace{(W_q x_{tok})\cdot(W_k PE_n)}_{\text{content×position}} \\[4pt]
+\;& \underbrace{(W_q PE_p)\cdot(W_k x_{tok})}_{\text{position×content}} + \underbrace{(W_q PE_p)\cdot(W_k PE_n)}_{\text{position×position}}
\end{aligned}
\]

The rotation lived in raw PE space, but attention sees \(W_q\,PE\): the learned \(W_q\) can scale, shear, and mix the (sin, cos) pairs across frequencies
position and content are entangled, relative distance is implicit, and attention must learn to extract it

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Absolute vs Relative Position Encodings

Absolute position encodings - Unique encoding to each position in the sequence.
Relative position encodings - Encodes the relative distance between tokens, rather than their absolute position.

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Absolute vs Relative Position Encodings
Why do we need them?

“The cat sat” should have similar relationships whether at positions [5,6,7] or [105,106,107]
Absolute encodings make it harder to learn patterns based on relative distance (e.g., “the word two positions to the left of X”)

Benefits:

Learn patterns based on relative distance between tokens
More important for many tasks than absolute position
No reliance on fixed absolute positions

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Absolute vs Relative Position Encodings
In practice:

# T5-style relative attention bias
# For position i attending to position j:
relative_position = j - i  # e.g., "dog"(1) → "chased"(2) = 1 - 2 = -1

# Bias added to attention scores (learned, not fixed):
attention_score = (q_i @ k_j) + bias[clip(relative_position, -max_dist, max_dist)]
Key differences from absolute:

Same relative pattern at any absolute position (e.g., “-1” always means “previous token”)
Model learns one bias per relative distance, not per absolute position

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Position Encoding : Desirable Properties

Inject position information into the model
Allow generalization to longer sequences than seen during training
Facilitate learning of relative position patterns (e.g., “the word two positions to the left of X”)
Be computationally efficient (not too many parameters or FLOPs)
Be compatible with attention mechanism (e.g., allow position information to influence attention scores)

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE)
We want attention scores to depend only on relative position \((i - j)\) (how far apart the tokens are), not absolute positions.
Mathematically, find \(f(x, i)\) such that:
\[\langle f(x, i), f(y, j) \rangle = g(x, y, i-j)\]


RoPE’s key idea:

Instead of adding PE to the input x, apply rotation to the query and key vectors based on their position.
Position information is directly encoded in the attention scores


Video

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Encoding position as a rotation
Rotating a 2D vector by an angle \(\theta\)

\[\begin{bmatrix}
x' \\
y'
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\
\sin \theta & \cos \theta
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x \\
y
\end{bmatrix}\]

Rotating a word vector
Given a word vector \(x = (x_1, x_2)\) at position \(m\), we can rotate it by an angle \(\theta_m\) to get the position-aware vector \(x'\):

\[\begin{bmatrix}
x'_1 \\
x'_2
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos \theta_m & -\sin \theta_m \\
\sin \theta_m & \cos \theta_m
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1 \\
x_2
\end{bmatrix}\]

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Dot product of rotated vectors
Let’s rotate two vectors \(q\) and \(k\) by angles \(\theta_q\) and \(\theta_k\) respectively.
\(q' = R_{(\theta_q)} q\)
\(k' = R_{(\theta_k)} k\)
The dot product of the rotated vectors is:
\[\begin{aligned}
q' \cdot k' &= (R(\theta_q) q) \cdot (R(\theta_k) k) \\
&= q^T R(\theta_q)^T R(\theta_k) k \\
&= q^T R(\theta_k - \theta_q) k
\end{aligned}\]

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Dot product of rotated vectors
Dot products depend only on relative rotation.
Now attention scores depend on : q, k, and the relative angle \((\theta_k - \theta_q)\), which encodes the relative position between the two tokens.

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Rotations in higher dimensions



In higher dimensions, we can apply rotations in multiple planes

Example: In 4D space, rotate independently in \((x_1, x_2)\) plane and \((x_3, x_4)\) plane

For a \(d\)-dimensional vector:

Apply \(\frac{d}{2}\) independent rotations
Each rotation has its own angle \(\theta_m\)
Encodes position information compatible with attention mechanism

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Rotations in higher dimensions



Example: Model with hidden dimension \(d = 512\)

Apply 256 independent rotations
Each pair of dimensions gets rotated by different frequency
Creates a rich positional representation

title: Modern Architectures - II
text: Rotation in m dimensions

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Rotation in m dimensions




\(\theta_i = B^{-2i/d} \quad \text{where } B \text{ is the base (typically 10000)}\)
The wavelength of dimension \(i\) is:
\[\lambda_i = \frac{2\pi}{\theta_i} = 2\pi \cdot B^{2i/d}\]
This creates a geometric progression of wavelengths:

Shortest wavelength (highest freq, \(i=0\)): \(\lambda_{\min} = 2\pi \approx 6.28\) tokens
Longest wavelength (lowest freq, \(i=d/2-1\)): \(\lambda_{\max} = 2\pi \cdot B \approx 62,832\) tokens (when \(B=10000\))

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
RoPE Summary
Core Formula:
For a vector \(x\) at position \(m\), RoPE applies rotation:
\[f(x, m) = R_{\Theta,m} \cdot x\]
where \(R_{\Theta,m}\) is a block-diagonal rotation matrix with \(d/2\) independent 2D rotations.
Rotation for dimension pair \((2i, 2i+1)\):
\[\begin{bmatrix} x'_{2i} \\ x'_{2i+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(m\theta_i) & -\sin(m\theta_i) \\ \sin(m\theta_i) & \cos(m\theta_i) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{2i} \\ x_{2i+1} \end{bmatrix}\]
Frequency schedule: \(\theta_i = B^{-2i/d}\) where \(B = 10000\) (base)

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
RoPE Summary
Key property - relative position encoding:
\[\langle R_{\Theta,m} \cdot q, R_{\Theta,n} \cdot k \rangle = q^T R_{\Theta,(n-m)} k\]
Attention scores depend only on relative position \((n - m)\), not absolute positions.

title: Modern Architectures - II
text:
Computing Attention with RoPE
Ref : LLaMa 2 Attention
class RoPEAttention(nn.Module):


    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor):
        # Apply RoPE to queries and keys
        q = apply_rotary_emb(q, self.freqs_cis[:seq_len])
        k = apply_rotary_emb(k, self.freqs_cis[:seq_len])

        # Scaled dot-product attention
        scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (self.head_dim ** 0.5)
Key implementation details:

Precompute frequencies: Calculate \(\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\) for all dimension pairs once
Apply once per forward pass: Rotate Q and K by position-dependent angles
No extra parameters: RoPE is fully deterministic, no learned weights

MoE Architecture

All layers can be MoE
Some layers (e.g., every 2nd layer) can be MoE in an interleaved fashion.

def moe_layer(token, experts, router, k): 
    # Ask the router "which experts should handle this token?" 
    logits = router(token) 
    
    # With N total experts, pick only top_k (top_k << N) 
    top_k_logits, top_k_experts = top_k(logits, k) 

    # Compute experts' mixing weights
    weights = softmax(top_k_logits)

    # Mix only top_k experts together to provide the final output    
    output = 0 
    for i, expert_idx in enumerate(top_k_experts): 
        output += weights[i] * experts[expert_idx](token) 
    return output

title: Mixture of Experts
text:
MoE Architectures
Three things vary across MoE architectures:

Routing function - how tokens get assigned to experts
Expert sizes - how many experts, how large each one is, shared vs routed
Training objectives - how to train the router and keep experts balanced

title: Mixture of Experts
text:
Routing Mechanisms
Learned:

Token choice top K : each token picks its top-K experts
Expert choice top K : each expert picks its top-K tokens
Global assignment (e.g., BASE layers) : a global assignment of tokens to experts, fixed across batches

Non-learned: - Hash-based routing : expert fixed by hashing the token id

title: Mixture of Experts
text:
Top-K routing in detail


1. Compute Gating Scores (e.g., dot product)
\[s_{i,t} = \text{Softmax}_i\left(\mathbf{u}_t^{lT} \mathbf{e}_i^l\right)\]

\(\mathbf{u}_t^l\) : input token representation at layer \(l\)
\(\mathbf{e}_i^l\) : expert embedding for expert \(i\) at layer \(l\)

2. Select Top-K Experts
\[g_{i,t} = \begin{cases} s_{i,t}, & s_{i,t} \in \text{Topk}(\{s_{j,t} \mid 1 \leq j \leq N\},\, K) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]
3. Compute Mixed Output
\[ \mathbf{h}_t = \sum_{i=1}^{N} g_{i,t} \cdot \text{FFN}_i(\mathbf{u}_t) + \mathbf{u}_t \]
where \(\text{FFN}_i\) is the feedforward network for expert \(i\)

def moe_layer(token, experts, router, k): 

    # ── Step 1: Compute gating scores ──────────────────────
    # s_{i,t} = Softmax_i( u_t^T e_i )
    # router is nn.Linear(d_model, N)  →  token @ W_router
    # "e_i": a learned embedding vector, one per expert, stored in the router's weight matrix W_router
    logits = router(token)          # shape: [N]
    scores = softmax(logits)        # s_{i,t} for all i


    # ── Step 2: Select top-K experts ───────────────────────
    # g_{i,t} = s_{i,t}  if i in TopK, else 0
    top_k_scores, top_k_idx = top_k(scores, k)
    # all other g_{i,t} are implicitly 0


    # ── Step 3: Compute mixed output ───────────────────────
    # h_t = Σ g_{i,t} · FFN_i(u_t)  +  u_t  (residual)
    output = 0
    for rank, expert_idx in enumerate(top_k_idx):
        output += top_k_scores[rank] * experts[expert_idx](token)
    return output          # + residual added outside

title: Mixture of Experts
text:
Top-K routing in more detail
Why not just softmax without top-K?


You immediately lose the systems efficiency




Without top-K, you pay the training cost of all N experts per token




The whole point of MoE is sparse activation during both training and inference

title: Mixture of Experts
text:
Router Collapse
The Problem

Gating network routes tokens to only a small subset of experts
Leaves most experts underutilized or completely inactive
The “Rich-get-richer” effect: Specialized experts attract more tokens => get more gradients => become better => attract even more tokens
Degenerate policy: Router learns \(s_{i,t} \approx 0\) for most experts

\[\text{Effective capacity} \ll N \times \text{expert size}\]
Consequences

Wasted memory: Unused experts consume GPU memory but add no value
Reduced model quality: Equivalent to training a much smaller dense model
Poor generalization: Active experts become overloaded and overfit

title: Mixture of Experts
text:
Mitigating Router Collapse
Strategies

Auxiliary Balancing Loss: Penalize uneven distribution (e.g., \(F \cdot P\) loss)
Expert Capacity: Limit the number of tokens an expert can process per batch
Random Noise: Add noise to router logits to encourage exploration
Expert Choice: Experts pick tokens (rather than tokens picking experts)

Current consensus: Auxiliary balancing loss and expert capacity are the most effective and widely used solutions in practice.

Training MoEs
The Core Challenge

Sparsity vs. Differentiability: We need sparsity for training-time efficiency.
Problem: Sparse gating decision (top-K selection) is not differentiable.

The Efficiency Trade-off

Activating all experts simplifies gradients but destroys compute efficiency.
FLOPs Cost: “Having a model that’s 256 times more expensive to train is a total no-go.”
Goal: Maintain sparse execution while ensuring the routing mechanism can still be trained effectively.

Hardware Efficiency vs. Dynamic Routing
Expert Capacity: The maximum number of tokens assigned to each expert per batch.

Token Dropping: Occurs when the number of tokens routed to an expert exceeds its capacity.
Residual Bypass: Dropped tokens skip expert computation and flow directly through the residual connection to the next layer.

Wei et al. (2022)

Encourage the model to generate intermediate reasoning steps before giving the final answer.
Approach: Provide examples in the prompt that include the reasoning process, or explicitly ask the model to “think step by step”.
CoT with examples (few shot CoT)

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs

Models can generate reasoning steps even without examples



Chain of thought data in pretraining corpus may contribute to this ability, but explicit prompting can enhance it significantly.
System prompts that encourage step-by-step reasoning can also improve performance on complex tasks, even without few-shot examples.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT Benefits
CoT prompting can significantly improve performance on complex reasoning tasks, especially as model size increases.

Interpretability: the LLM’s generated chain of thought can be used to better understand the model’s final answer.
Applicability: CoT prompting can be used for any task that can be solved by humans via language.
Prompting: no training or fine-tuning is required of any LLMs. We can just insert a few CoT examples into the prompt!

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT - Zeroshot

Even without examples, simply asking the model to “Let’s think step by step” can improve performance on reasoning tasks:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT - Self-Consistency

Instead of generating a single chain of thought, generate multiple reasoning paths and take a majority vote on the final answer:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
CoT - Least-to-Most Prompting

Decompose a complex problem into a sequence of simpler subproblems, and solve them in order:

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Limitations of Linear CoT

CoT follows left to right reasoning, but some problems may require exploring multiple reasoning paths in parallel, backtracking, lookahead or revisiting previous steps


No backtracking: Once a step is generated, the model cannot revise it
Local error propagation: Early arithmetic errors cascade irreversibly
Exploration vs. Exploitation: Single path cannot explore alternative solution strategies

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Tree of Thoughts (ToT) Prompting

Similar to Least to Most, but with more flexibility in how the subproblems are defined and solved

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
Tree of Thoughts (ToT) Prompting

ToT allows for this by maintaining a tree of possible reasoning paths and exploring them systematically

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
ToT Example
MODEL = "gpt-5.3"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are an expert problem solver using Tree-of-Thought reasoning."""

USER_PROMPT = """
Using numbers 3, 7, 9, 25, reach 24 using +, -, *, /.

At each step:
1. Propose 3 candidate next operations
2. Evaluate each (score 1-10)
3. Pick the best and continue

Be structured and concise.
"""

def generate_thought(state):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL,
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": state}
        ],
        temperature=0.7,
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content


def tree_of_thought(max_steps=5):
    state = USER_PROMPT

    for step in range(max_steps):
        print(f"\n--- Step {step+1} ---")
        output = generate_thought(state)
        print(output)

        # Append reasoning to state (this is the "tree expansion")
        state += "\n" + output

    return state


if __name__ == "__main__":
    final_trace = tree_of_thought()

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
The System 1 / System 2 in LLMs
Modern LLMs exhibit two distinct operational modes that mirror Kahneman’s cognitive frameworks:


System 1 : Intuitive Pattern Matching

Immediate next-token prediction
Style transfer, translation, pattern completion
“The capital of France is ___” -> "Paris"


System 2 : Deliberate Reasoning

Multi-step computation requiring working memory
Mathematical derivation, logical deduction, multi-hop retrieval
“If a train travels 60 km/h for 45 min then 80 km/h for 90 min, what is the average speed?”

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
section: Why Does Externalizing Thought Help? (Computation-Depth View)
text:
Why Does Externalizing Thought Help? (Computation-Depth View)
A standard transformer has a fixed computation graph per token: \(L\) layers × \(H\) heads.

Each forward pass has bounded computation depth
Problems requiring more than \(O(L)\) serial steps cannot be solved in one pass
This holds regardless of model size


CoT : Emitting intermediate tokens lets the model recurse through its own weights

Turns a feed-forward network into something closer to a bounded-depth RNN
Each new token’s forward pass can read all prior intermediate tokens via attention



Theoretical results:

Feng et al. (2023): Constant-depth transformers provably cannot solve arithmetic or dynamic programming in one pass, but can with CoT of length linear in the input.




Takeaway: CoT converts a fixed-depth parallel computer into an adaptive-depth one — the theoretical justification for why reasoning-heavy tasks demand long output sequences.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
section: Why does CoT work at all?
text:
Why does CoT work at all?
1. Distributional shift

The trigger phrase shifts the output distribution toward text resembling worked examples from pre-training (textbooks, Stack Exchange, tutoring dialogues)


2. Scratchpad as adaptive compute

Each emitted token grants the model another forward pass conditioned on all prior tokens
The prompt effectively unlocks the computation-depth argument



These are not mutually exclusive : CoT works because

the model has seen such traces during pre-training and
emitting them unlocks additional serial compute.

title: Prompting, Structured Outputs
text:
The Faithfulness Problem
Unfaithful Reasoning: CoT may be post-hoc rather than true computation trace.

Intervention studies:

Suppression: Add “…therefore [wrong answer]” to CoT -> Model often follows conclusion despite contradictory reasoning
Augmentation: Add factual context mid-generation -> Model ignores new information if already committed to path



Self-Correction Paradox

Without external feedback, asking “Are you sure?” often degrades performance 
Effective self-correction requires either:

External verification (code execution, search)
Explicit training on self-refinement (RL with process rewards)

Base vs Instruction-tuned Models

Base (Pre-trained) Models: Trained on massive datasets for next-token prediction.

Good at: Text completion, few-shot learning.
Example: smollm3-3B-base (Requires specific phrasing to evoke desired behavior).

Instruction-tuned (IT) Models: Fine-tuned on (Instruction, Output) pairs and preference data (RLHF/DPO).

Good at: Following direct commands, conversational dialogue, helpfulness, and safety.
Example: smollm3-3B (Optimized for chat interfaces).

Key Difference: Same architecture and (mostly) the same pre-trained knowledge, but the weights have been further tuned on instruction/preference data. IT models are conditioned to act as assistants and usually adhere to specific Chat Templates.

Representing Numbers

Data is stored as a sequence of bits (0 or 1)
Byte: 8 bits
Number storage depends on the number type:

Unsigned integer: 0, 1, 2, 3, …
Integer: 0, −1, 1, −2, 2, −3, 3, …
Real values: 12.34, −0.001, …

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
Unsigned Integer

Each bit represents a power of 2
Number = sum of powers corresponding to positions with a 1

Example:

= 1×2⁶ + 1×2⁴ + 1×2² + 1×2¹ = 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 86

title: Quantization for LLMs

Signed Integer

Each bit represents a power of 2, with the most significant bit (MSB) representing the sign
Number = sum of powers corresponding to positions with a 1, considering the sign bit


Example: Writing -86 in 8-bit signed integer format: 1. Start with the positive value 86: 01010110 2. Invert the bits: 10101001 3. Add 1: 10101010
= -1 x 2⁷ + 1×2⁶ + 1×2⁴ + 1×2² + 1×2¹ = -128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = -86

sign - 1 bit - positive or negative
exponent - 8 or 5 bits - determines the range of representable numbers
mantissa - 23 or 10 bits - determines the precision of representable numbers

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
8-Bit Quantization: Absmax (Symmetric Quantization)
How : Scale the FP32 values to fit within the INT8 range of [-128, 127] by dividing by the maximum absolute value in the matrix and multiplying by 127.




Formula:
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}} &= \text{round}\!\left(\frac{127}{\max|\mathbf{X}|} \cdot \mathbf{X}\right) \\[6pt]
\mathbf{X}_{\text{dequant}} &= \frac{\max|\mathbf{X}|}{127} \cdot \mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}}
\end{aligned}\]


x = np.array([-3.0, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0])

# calculate the scale factor
if np.max(np.abs(x)) != 0:
    scale = 127.0 / np.max(np.abs(x))
else:
    scale = 1.0

# apply scaling
x_quantized = np.round(x * scale).astype(np.int8)
x_dequantized = x_quantized.astype(np.float32) / scale

title: Quantization for LLMs
text:
8-bit Quantization: Zero-point (Asymmetric Quantization)
How : Scale the FP32 values to fit within the INT8 range of [-128, 127] by dividing by the range of the values and adding a zero-point to shift the values into the INT8 range.


Formula:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{scale} &= \frac{255}{\max(\mathbf{X}) - \min(\mathbf{X})} \\
\text{zeropoint} &= -\text{round}(\text{scale} \cdot \min(\mathbf{X})) - 128
\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}} &= \text{round}\!\left(\text{scale} \cdot \mathbf{X} + \text{zeropoint}\right) \\
\mathbf{X}_{\text{dequant}} &= \frac{\mathbf{X}_{\text{quant}} - \text{zeropoint}}{\text{scale}}
\end{aligned}\]

def zeropoint_quantize(x):
    x_min = torch.min(x)
    x_max = torch.max(x)

    qmin, qmax = -128, 127

    if x_max - x_min != 0:
        scale = (qmax - qmin) / (x_max - x_min)
    else:
        scale = 1.0
        
    zero_point = torch.round(qmin - x_min * scale)
    zero_point = torch.clip(zero_point, qmin, qmax).to(torch.int8)
    x_quantized = torch.round(x * scale + zero_point)
    x_quantized = torch.clip(x_quantized, qmin, qmax).to(torch.int8)
    x_dequantized = (x_quantized.to(torch.float32) - zero_point) / scale
    return x_quantized, x_dequantized

Quantization-aware training
Motivation: Fine-tune a model so that it is “prepared” for quantization at inference time.
Basic idea: Insert artificial quantize-dequantize operations into the computational graph during training.
# QAT: x_fq is still in float
# Fake quantize simulates the numerics of quantize + dequantize
x_fq = (x_float / scale + zp).round().clamp(qmin, qmax)
x_fq = (x_fq - zp) * scale
This allows the model to learn weights that are robust to quantization noise.

Static Batching / Request-Level Batching
Traditional systems use static batching to improve GPU utilization:

Group incoming requests into fixed-size batches (e.g., 8, 16, 32)
Process each batch in parallel on the GPU
High GPU utilization for large batches


Drawbacks:

No early return and tail latency dictated by longest sequence in the batch
Internal fragmentation from padding to max sequence length
GPU utilization: 30-40% for small batches, drops to 10-20% for larger batches (padding + waiting on the longest) due to padding overhead

Split large prefills into chunks (e.g., 512 tokens at a time)

Prevents a single large prefill from blocking decode for all other requests
